Chronicle & Archive

Eight Centuries of Grace Dieu

From a secluded Roman-traversed Charnwood valley to a pioneering independent Augustinian nunnery, a Jacobean literary cradle, and a volunteer-rescued monument.

Although the land surrounding Grace Dieu possesses ancient heritage connections dating back to the Romans and beyond, the Priory came into being between 1235 and 1241 as a house for Augustinian canonesses. Dedicated to God, the Holy Trinity, and St Mary, it was founded by the remarkable Norman-Irish noblewoman Rohese (Rose) de Verdon.

Rose belonged to a prominent feudal dynasty with substantial manorial holdings across Leicestershire and Ireland. Her father, Nicholas de Verdon, had received the lands around Snape from William Wastneis, Lord of Osgathorpe, to extend his deer park at Belton. When no male heir survived, Rose took direct charge of the estates, paying King Henry III a fine to rule in her own right. In the sheltered Charnwood dale along the Grace Dieu Brook, she established a sanctuary of contemplation, hospitality, and prayer.

Foundation Charter Confirmation · 1241
“The church of the Holy Trinity of the Grace of God at Belton dedicated to God and St Mary”

— Confirmation Charter granted by Bishop Robert Grosseteste of Lincoln (1241), giving the priory its enduring epithet Gratia Dei (Grace Dieu).

Rose endowed the priory with “all my manor of Belton… the park, warren and mills” alongside the Manor of Kirby in Kesteven, Lincolnshire. She was buried upon her death in 1247 in the priory church, and monastic records specify that an annual sum of 12d was dedicated to maintain a perpetual light burning over her tomb.

At the 1538 Dissolution, local parishioners reverently salvaged Rose’s sculpted tomb and effigy, transferring her memorial to the parish church of St John the Baptist in Belton, where it remains preserved and admired today.

Founder Tomb: St John the Baptist Church, Belton (2 miles away)
Talks on Rohese de Verdon’s Life›
Preserved Relic

13th-Century Carved Ashlar

Finely chiselled Charnwood stone fragment demonstrating the high quality of early English Gothic craftsmanship achieved by Rose’s masons.

ERA I (1235–1538)

The Augustinian Nunnery

Three centuries of monastic prayer, agricultural estate management, and community care in the Charnwood valley.

c. 1235–1241FOUNDING CHARTER

The Founding of Gratia Dei

Rohese (Rose) de Verdon, a powerful Norman-Irish noblewoman holding independent feudal authority, established the priory in the secluded Charnwood valley as an autonomous house of Augustinian canonesses dedicated to God, the Holy Trinity, and St Mary. The earliest recorded prioresses were Agnes de Gresley (1240) and Mary de Stretton (1243), who guided the nascent community through its early material welfare and spiritual foundations.

✦ Confirmed by Bishop Robert Grosseteste of Lincoln, granting the nuns independent governance free from external monastic subjection.

1306LAND EXPANSION

The Forest Gift of John Comyn

John Comyn, Earl of Buchan and Lord of Whitwick, granted the priory 100 acres of newly cleared forest waste situated at Whitwick and Shepshed. This major territorial addition secured valuable woodland pasture, grazing rights, and timber for the canonesses, forming the geographic foundation of the modern priory parkland and ancient woodland footpaths enjoyed today.

✦ Established the pastoral estate boundaries that define the secluded Charnwood monument setting.

1377COMMUNITY CARE

Expansion & The Almonry Hospital

By 1377, the priory community had expanded to 16 professed canonesses. In keeping with their Augustinian charitable rule, the sisters maintained an almonry hospital within the precinct. The hospital provided shelter, warm meals, and daily hospice care to 12 poor and destitute individuals from the surrounding Charnwood parishes, making the priory an indispensable social lifeline.

✦ Provided healthcare and sustenance to 12 destitute local parishioners for nearly two centuries.

1414–1418MANUSCRIPT ARCHIVE

Dame Petronella’s Account Book

During the prioress-ship of Dame Petronella, working draft accounts were meticulously kept by Dame Petronella and her assistant Dame Katherine Midleton. Surviving today in the Public Record Office, this 348-page manuscript details tenant rent collections across Leicestershire (including Belton lands generating £21 17s 9d), inventories of pigs and cattle, fish sales from the Belton watermill weir bringing in £6, building repair wages, and food provisions for holy feast days.

✦ An internationally celebrated working draft revealing the everyday tangible economic realities of early 15th-century monastic life.

Order the Published Account Book in our Shop (£15)›
1535–1538HENRICIAN DISSOLUTION

Valuation, Reprieve & Suppression

In 1535, the priory’s net annual income was assessed at approximately £92. A year later, King Henry VIII’s visiting commissioners, Drs Leigh and Layton, arrived and issued a reduced valuation of £72 13s 4d. Because of this lower threshold, Grace Dieu was slated for closure under the 1536 Act for the Suppression of Lesser Monasteries. Although the priory secured a temporary royal reprieve due to its exemplary reputation, the respite was brief: King Henry VIII’s commissioners formally dissolved the monastery in October 1538.

✦ The final prioress, Agnes Litherland, surrendered the priory keys; pensions were granted to fifteen remaining sisters.

Romantic Poetry · Coleorton Hall
“Beneath yon eastern ridge, the craggy bound,
Rugged and high, of Charnwood’s forest ground,
Stand yet, but, Stranger, hidden from thy view
The ivied ruins of forlorn Grace Dieu,
Erst a religious House, which day and night
With hymns resounded and the chanted rite.”
— William Wordsworth

Written while staying with his friend and patron, Sir George Beaumont, at nearby Coleorton Hall

ERA II (1539–1700s)

The Beaumont Dynasty & The Tudor Mansion

How royal commissioners, Elizabethan judges, and Jacobean dramatists transformed the sacred cloisters into a literary country seat.

1534–1552 · SURVEYOR & MASTER

John Beaumont & The Mansion Conversion

Grandson of Thomas Beaumont of Coleorton, John Beaumont was appointed by King’s Writ in January 1534–5 to take the ecclesiastical survey of Leicestershire monasteries. In 1539, after the priory was valued at £125 and granted to the Earl of Huntingdon, it passed to Beaumont.

Beaumont ingeniously remodeled the nunnery cloisters into a grand Tudor mansion, erecting the massive brick chimneys that still stand. Under Edward VI in 1550 he rose to Master of the Rolls, though financial forfeiture in 1552 briefly cost the family their estates until his widow, Elizabeth Hastings, successfully reclaimed Grace Dieu.

✦ Transformed the religious house into a courtier’s family residence.

D. 1598 · ELIZABETHAN JUDGE

Francis Beaumont, Justice of Common Pleas

Following Elizabeth’s death in 1588, her eldest son Francis succeeded to the estate. Educated in the law, he became an eminent Elizabethan legal figure and Justice of the Court of Common Pleas, presiding over major judicial circuits.

He resided continuously at Grace Dieu until his death on April 22, 1598. He and his wife Anne Pierrepoint raised four remarkable children in the cloistered home: Sir Henry, Sir John, Elizabeth, and Francis—nurturing an environment rich in poetry, drama, and classical learning.

✦ Established Grace Dieu as a distinguished legal and intellectual estate.

EARLY 1600s · DRAMA & POETRY

The Jacobean Poets & Dramatists

Francis Beaumont (1584–1616) of the Inner Temple became one of England’s most celebrated dramatists, co-authoring 35 renowned plays with John Fletcher for the King’s Men. He died aged 30 and was accorded burial in Poets’ Corner, Westminster Abbey.

His elder brother, Sir John Beaumont (1583–1627), was created 1st Baronet in 1626 and authored the acclaimed epic poem “Bosworth Field”, celebrating regional history. He is buried in the parish church at Belton.

✦ Grace Dieu’s sons helped shape English literature in Shakespeare’s era.

The Civil War, Decline & 17th-Century Demolition

From Cavalier Tragedy to Romantic Ruin

The English Civil War brought tragedy to the Beaumont family. Francis’s grandson, Sir John Beaumont (born 1607), served as a loyal colonel in King Charles I’s army and was slain in battle at the Siege of Gloucester in 1644. His brother Sir Thomas Beaumont lived at Grace Dieu until his death in 1686 (buried at Belton), having eight daughters, which caused the baronetcy to become extinct.

The estate was sold in 1690 to Sir Ambrose Phillipps, Knight of Garendon and King’s Serjeant. Seeking to harvest stone and discourage tenant residence, Phillipps intentionally pulled down the former priory church and dismantled parts of the house. The property passed through his son William, grandson Samuel, and Thomas March Phillipps, while nature gradually reclaimed the stone cloisters with Charnwood ivy.

ERA III (1995–PRESENT)

Conservation & Modern Custodianship

How two decades of voluntary determination saved collapsing masonry and secured permanent ownership for future generations.

1995–2006 · VOLUNTEER SALVATION

The 10-Year Emergency Masonry Rescue

By 1995, Grace Dieu was an abandoned pile of stone shrouded in tonnes of choking ivy, saplings, and briars, facing catastrophic collapse. A dedicated group of local residents banded together to save what remained, establishing The Grace Dieu Priory Charitable Trust.

Between 1996 and 2006, master stonemasons and volunteers cleared vegetation, secured failing Gothic arches with lime mortar and stainless steel ties, and consolidated the surviving ruins without synthetic cement. In 2006, the site was officially opened to the public free of charge, with The Friends of Grace Dieu Priory (Charity No. 1117921) formed to conduct day-to-day stewardship, educational visits, and guided walks.

✦ Rescued from total loss entirely through public support, charitable donations, and community volunteer labour.

2024 · HISTORIC FREEHOLD ACQUISITION

Permanent Freehold Site Ownership Secured

In November 2024, following two years of sensitive negotiations with private landowners, The Grace Dieu Priory Trust officially completed the freehold purchase of the entire monument and Rusty Mary’s field.

Having previously cared for the site as tenants, the Trust now possesses permanent statutory authority. In partnership with the Charnwood Forest Geopark, volunteers have already uncovered lengths of the original 800-year-old boundary wall. Freehold ownership empowers the charity to launch new scheduled archaeological digs and construct a permanent accessible footbridge from Rusty Mary’s field into the cloisters.

✦ Guarantees perpetual protection and free community access for generations to come.

Visitor Code

Leave No TracePlease take all of your litter home with you. There are no public waste bins on the ancient monument ruins.
Dog WalkersDogs welcome on leads. A dedicated bin is located at the Bull's Head car park for dog litter bags (strictly none on-site).
Strict Site Policy: Paranormal events and ghost walks are expressly forbidden by the Grace Dieu Priory Trust across the entire priory site and surrounding lands.
